blocks.text: In JavaScript, Python and Java, a string is **immutable**: once it exists, its characters can never change. Every operation that seems to change a string — upper-casing, replacing, appending — actually builds a **new** string and leaves the old one untouched. C++ is the exception: a `std::string` can be edited in place.

blocks.code:
s = "hello"; then try s[0] = 'J'

JavaScript   s[0] = "J"   is silently ignored (a TypeError in strict mode); s is still "hello"
Python       s[0] = "J"   raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
Java         there is no method that sets a character; s.replace(...) returns a new String
C++          s[0] = 'J';  works: s is now "Jello"

items: **Safe sharing.** Two variables can point at the same text, and neither can surprise the other by changing it.
**Fast hashing.** A string that can't change can compute its hash once and cache it, which makes strings excellent hash-map keys.
**One copy of repeated text.** Identical literals like `"OK"` can share one object in memory (Java calls this the string pool).
**Thread safety.** Several threads can read the same string with no locks.

blocks.text: Because a string can't grow, `s += piece` must allocate a **new** string and copy the whole of `s` into it, then the piece. Do that in a loop and the copying adds up: building a string of n characters one at a time copies 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n characters — about n² / 2. That's **O(n²)** for what looks like a simple loop.

blocks.alt: Building abcd one character at a time with +=. Step 1 makes a, copying 1 character. Step 2 makes a new string ab, copying 2. Step 3 makes abc, copying 3. Step 4 makes abcd, copying 4. In total 10 characters are copied to build 4. A builder writes each character once: 4.

elements.text: grey: copied again from the old string    green: the new character

blocks.text: Some runtimes soften this — modern JavaScript engines and CPython can sometimes extend a string in place — but neither guarantees it, and Java's `+=` in a loop really does copy each time. In an interview, assume `+=` on a string in a loop is O(n²).
The fix is the same idea in every language: collect the pieces in something that **can** grow cheaply, then make the final string **once**.

items: **JavaScript** — push pieces into an array, then `parts.join("")`.
**Python** — append pieces to a list, then `"".join(parts)`.
**Java** — `StringBuilder`: `append(...)` is amortized O(1), like `ArrayList.add`, and `toString()` copies once at the end.
**C++** — `std::string` itself is the builder: `s += piece` and `s.push_back(c)` append in place, amortized O(1). (But `s = s + piece` still builds a full temporary copy.)

blocks.text: Here are both ways of joining words with single spaces. (Each language also has a one-liner — `words.join(" ")`, `" ".join(words)`, `String.join(" ", words)` — which builds in O(n) exactly like approach 2.)

blocks.caption: Every += makes a whole new string. Watch the copy counter grow faster than the string.

blocks.text: **Time O(n²), space O(n)** for a result of n characters: every append copies all the characters so far.
**Time O(n), space O(n).** Each character is written into the buffer once (plus the occasional doubling of the buffer, which averages out to O(1) per character), and copied once more at the end.

blocks.alt: Repeated +=: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Builder / join: O(n) time, O(n) space.

blocks.text: When a question asks you to modify a string in place — reverse it, swap characters, replace some — turn it into an **array of characters** first, change the array, and turn it back at the end:

blocks.code:
JavaScript   const a = [...s];        ... a[i] = x ...   a.join("")
Python       a = list(s)              ... a[i] = x ...   "".join(a)
Java         char[] a = s.toCharArray();  ... a[i] = x ...   new String(a)
C++          s[i] = x;                (std::string is already mutable)

blocks.text: Converting costs O(n) once, and every change after that is O(1). Many interview questions skip this step by handing you the characters as an array already — Reverse String in the next chapter is one.
